title: Retrieval: Week Three
focus: The hardest week to recall, which is exactly why it is the most valuable retrieval day of the month.

cards.title: Arrays and Strings: blind recall
cards.trigger: Binary search stopped being about arrays this week. That reframing is the thing to keep.
cards.recall: Paper: the feasibility-search skeleton, the bucket-by-frequency loop, the rotated-array half test, the two-sweep prefix and suffix, quickselect's partition, and the trapping-water two-pointer. Then say which of the six is the one you would still fumble.
template: # Binary search, three faces:
#   1. index in a sorted array          -> lower_bound
#   2. index in a ROTATED array         -> find the sorted half first
#   3. a VALUE, via feasible(x)         -> minimise the maximum
# Selection, three faces:
#   sorted output needed  -> sort, O(n log n)
#   top k, any order      -> quickselect, O(n) average
#   streaming             -> size-k heap, O(n log k)
keyInsights: Binary search on the answer is the highest-leverage pattern of the whole month. It converts hard problems into easy predicates
Quickselect mutates and does not order. Heap does neither. Read the constraints and pick deliberately
Two-sweep prefix and suffix replaces division, and generalises to any 'everything except me' aggregate
cards.trap: Saying binary search on the answer is O(log n). It is O(n log(range)). This is the follow-up you will actually be asked.

cards.title: Structures and Design: blind recall
cards.trigger: This week's structures are the ones people skip. Skipping them is why they fail the hard round.
cards.recall: From memory: the swap-with-last removal, wildcard trie DFS, both Fenwick loops, the timestamp binary search, and the histogram stack with its width formula. The Fenwick loops and the histogram width are the two most forgettable lines in the entire program.

drill.name: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

template: i += i & -i    # BIT update: walk up
i -= i & -i    # BIT query:  walk down
width = i - stack[-1] - 1   # histogram, after popping, with -1 if empty
# Range query decision:
#   static, sums only ......... prefix array
#   point update, sums ........ Fenwick
#   point update, min/max/gcd . segment tree
#   range update .............. segment tree with lazy propagation
keyInsights: The range-query decision table is four lines and it answers a whole category of interview questions
The histogram width formula is the single most error-prone line this week. Write it three times today
Fenwick is half the code of a segment tree and covers most real questions. Default to it when the aggregate is a sum
cards.trap: Writing a Fenwick tree 0-indexed. `i & -i` is zero at index 0 and the update loop never terminates its first step. It must be 1-indexed.

cards.title: Trees: blind recall
cards.trigger: This week the tree stopped being rooted. Distance from an arbitrary node needs parent edges.
cards.recall: From memory: is_same plus is_subtree, BST delete's three cases, the flatten predecessor splice, the mirror cross-comparison, the parent-map BFS, and coordinate traversal with its tie-break.

drill.name: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List

template: # Two symmetric facts worth pairing in memory:
#   BST delete   -> LEFTMOST of the RIGHT subtree (inorder successor)
#   tree flatten -> RIGHTMOST of the LEFT subtree (preorder predecessor)
# And the fourth tree shape, added this week:
#   convert to an undirected graph (parent map), then ordinary BFS
keyInsights: The successor and predecessor pairing is easy to confuse and easy to remember once paired deliberately
The moment the question says 'distance from node X', build parent links. Do not try to be clever
Coordinate traversals are BFS carrying extra numbers. The only hard part is the tie-break rule
cards.trap: Assuming BFS order resolves ties in vertical order traversal. That is the easier lookalike problem. Read which one you are on.

cards.title: DP: blind recall
cards.trigger: Three new shapes this week: state machine, interval, and bitmask. Name the shape before the state.
cards.recall: For each, name the shape first, then the state sentence, then the recurrence. Draw the stock state machine. Say why burst balloons loops over the last move. Say what n makes bitmask viable.

drill.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell with Cooldown
Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

template: # The DP shape catalogue so far:
#   linear        dp[i]        from a fixed lookback
#   grid          dp[r][c]     from already-computed neighbours
#   two-sequence  dp[i][j]     over two prefixes
#   knapsack      dp[capacity] loop direction decides reuse
#   state machine dp[mode]     named modes, simultaneous update
#   interval      dp[i][j]     over a RANGE, fill by increasing length
#   bitmask       dp[mask]     subset as an integer, n <= ~20
# Name the shape first. The state sentence follows from the shape.
keyInsights: Seven shapes cover essentially every DP you will be asked. Naming the shape is faster than deriving from scratch
Interval DP fills by increasing length. Every other shape fills by increasing index. That is the thing to remember
When greedy works, you must be able to prove it. When you cannot prove it, write the DP
cards.trap: Reaching for interval DP on burst balloons but framing it as first-move. It compiles, it runs, and it is wrong. The last-move framing is the problem.

cards.title: Graphs and Backtracking: blind recall
cards.trigger: Backtracking is a graph search where the graph is your choices. Same skeleton, four times this week.
cards.recall: From memory: the permutation used-array plus the duplicate skip, combination sum's reuse index, word search's mark and unmark, N-Queens' three sets, the clone map registered before recursing, and the wildcard bucket BFS.
template: # One backtracking skeleton, four dressings:
def go(state):
if complete(state): record(); return
for choice in options(state):
if not allowed(choice): continue     # PRUNE here, not after
apply(choice)
go(next_state)
undo(choice)                         # every apply needs an undo
# subsets/combinations -> options start at `start`, no undo of a used-array
# permutations         -> used[] array, undo it
# grid path            -> mark the cell, undo the mark
# constraints          -> conflict sets, undo all of them
keyInsights: Every apply needs exactly one undo. Missing one gives wrong output rather than an error, which is the worst kind of bug
Prune inside the loop before recursing. Pruning after the recursive call does nothing
Implicit graphs, word ladder and lock puzzles, are ordinary BFS. Do not let the lack of an adjacency list disguise them
cards.trap: Permutations with duplicates using `used[i-1]` instead of `not used[i-1]`. Both produce output. Only one is correct.
